title: India Proposes Red Warning Labels on Packaged Food After Supreme Court Pressure
excerpt: FSSAI reverses course to mandate hexagonal warning symbols for high sugar, fat, and salt products in a setback for Coca-Cola, Nestle, and PepsiCo
body:
• FSSAI has proposed red hexagonal warning labels for packaged foods high in two or more of saturated fat, sugar, or salt, filed with the Supreme Court on Friday
  • The reversal follows public anger after Reuters revealed companies like Coca-Cola sell products with three times more sugar in India than in the UK
  • Maharashtra food commissioner Tukaram Mundhe urged companies to maintain the same standards in India as abroad, calling the disparity unethical

India's food safety regulator has proposed mandatory front-of-pack warning labels on packaged food and drinks, reversing a position it adopted under industry pressure earlier this year. The proposal, filed in the Supreme Court on Friday, marks a significant defeat for multinational food companies that had lobbied against the measure for years.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India said it would require a red-coloured hexagonal warning symbol on products that are high in two or more nutrients — saturated fat, sugar, or salt — according to the filing seen by Reuters. Labels would declare warnings such as "HIGH FAT," "HIGH SUGAR," "HIGH SALT," and "HIGHLY SWEETENED BEVERAGE."

Corporate Lobbying and the March Meeting

The proposal comes after a turbulent week in India's food policy debate. Reuters reported earlier this week that companies including Coca-Cola, Nestle, and PepsiCo successfully lobbied FSSAI to drop a similar proposal following a tense meeting in March. A senior Coca-Cola India executive argued at that meeting that warning labels were pointless because they would not prevent consumers from having sugary foods, and that Indian doctors had done an adequate job advising patients on diet.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=GJ4xiPYPyHE

FSSAI had buckled under the pressure, telling the Supreme Court in August that matching international labelling standards was "difficult." The court responded sharply, saying "the world should know that India is very much concerned about the overall health of its citizens."

"Warning labels don't insult consumer intelligence, they respect it. The argument that doctors already advise patients misses the point: prevention should not depend on already being sick."

— Tukaram Mundhe, Maharashtra Food Commissioner

Double Standards Under Scrutiny

The debate intensified after Reuters revealed that global food companies maintain different formulations for the same products in India and Western markets. A can of Fanta sold in London contains 63 calories, while the same-sized product in India packs 185 calories — three times the sugar content. These companies voluntarily display front-of-pack warning labels in European markets but have resisted mandatory labels in India's over $100 billion packaged food market.

Tukaram Mundhe, Maharashtra's food commissioner who has become India's most prominent food safety enforcer through raids on establishments including Domino's and McDonald's, was the first government official to comment on the discrepancy.

"Where are ethics in this? Companies should not only abide with legal compliances but also practice ethical behaviour. Why the different standard," Mundhe told Reuters. "They have responsibility towards society."

A Public Health Crisis

Industry estimates suggest nearly 80 percent of products in India's packaged food market could qualify as high in fat, sugar, or salt — meaning most packaging would carry red warning labels if the proposal is implemented.

The health stakes are stark. Around 450 million Indians could be obese or overweight by 2050, according to a study published in The Lancet. India already has roughly 101 million people with diabetes, making it the world's diabetes capital, per a 2023 Indian Council of Medical Research study.

Currently, manufacturers are required only to list ingredients and basic nutritional information on the back of packaging — a format that health advocates say most consumers never read.

What Happens Next

The FSSAI's filing said labels would be implemented in phases to give the industry time to comply. Single-ingredient food products would be exempted. However, the proposal requires products to be high in at least two nutrients to trigger a warning — a weaker standard than Israel's system, which the Supreme Court had suggested as a model, where a single high nutrient is enough.

Nestle's global CEO said this week that the company wants India to consult manufacturers when drafting the rules to ensure they are done "scientifically." Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, and Nestle did not respond to requests for comment on Mundhe's remarks.

For Indian consumers — and millions of diaspora families who regularly send or receive packaged food products from India — the labelling shift could fundamentally change how they assess what goes into their grocery baskets.
